rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and methods / Results <U+2013> authors collected their own 2018 time-series of UAV RGB mosaics, EMI soil ECa surveys, in-situ soil moisture sensors, soil samples and combine-harvester yield data on a 20 ha soybean field in Arkansas and analysed their co-variability.
rows.notes: The study's own result is that UAV-derived plant spatial abundance, vigor (GCC) and height maps identify persistent anomalous (low-productivity) areas, and that these anomalies are controlled by soil clay content (high ECa) and by a soil-moisture decline tied to topography and non-uniform furrow irrigation (Fig. 9, Tables 2-3). It does not detect or attribute any abnormality to pests, diseases or nutrient deficiencies, which are the abnormalities named in the passage, and it does not test interventions or production gains following detection. Because the detected abnormalities are of a different nature (soil texture/moisture) than those claimed, Q2 is answered no; the study offers at most generic support that UAV imagery can flag anomalous growth areas.

rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and methods / Results <U+2013> own UAV, EMI, soil-sensor, soil-sample and yield data from a commercial soybean field in Arkansas, 2018 season.
rows.notes: The study contains no IoT-connected sprayers, no targeted fertilizer or pesticide application, no measurement of chemical use, and no assessment of crop health response to an intervention. Its own result is limited to mapping anomalous plant-development zones from UAV imagery (SVM classification of plants vs soil, GCC vigor, SfM plant height) and relating them to soil ECa, soil moisture and yield. Identifying affected zones from imagery is at most a precondition of the claimed targeted-application effect, so upstream is set to true.

rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and methods / Results <U+2013> own UAV, EMI, soil-sensor, soil-sample and yield data from a commercial soybean field in Arkansas, 2018 season.
rows.notes: No pests or pest infestations are observed, detected or treated in the study; the anomalous zones identified by UAV imagery are attributed to soil clay content and soil-moisture/irrigation non-uniformity, not to pests, and no pesticide or sprayer is involved. The study therefore provides no evidence on pest control via image-guided targeted spraying; its image-based zone identification is at most an upstream precondition.

notes: Full text appears complete (abstract through references). Primary field study integrating UAV RGB imagery and EMI geophysics on one soybean field for one season; supplementary figures not included but not needed for these ratings. None of the three claims (pest/disease/nutrient detection, IoT targeted spraying, pest control) is addressed by the study's own results.
